synopsis: Variant management must support confidence across machine configurations and operating conditions; historically, comparable braking-function validation took three to four years, largely through physical testing and tuning per machine model [f31, f282, f1174]. The proposed reuse strategy is a parameterized machine-family model validated at envelope corners, with configuration-controlled deltas and targeted bridge tests for each new variant; physics-based families should be identified before the 2027 hardware arrives [f190, f7573, f7908, f6124]. Reuse cannot rest on sensor validation alone, because braking architecture, latency, mass, payload, implements and software integration change outcomes, and the reported mining regime requires separate verification of machines with different braking characteristics [f3437, f5181]. Evidence reuse is potentially a major lever, but no published quantified time-saving case, safe number of removable physical tests, or ISO rule validating a family through N representative machines was found [f617, f261, f1960, f6683]. Even 2,995 independent zero-miss opportunities support only an aggregate detection-at-least-99.9% claim at 95% confidence for a defined population, not sufficient evidence for an entire product family [f6885]. Planning should explicitly delimit covered variants and exclusions, consider an initial release split by machine family with a restricted operating envelope, and establish which subsequent changes trigger partial or full revalidation [f10155, f12326, f10365].
